name: Cell-assisted lipotransfer (CAL)

card.summary: A fat-grafting method that enriches a patient's own transferred fat with adipose-derived stem/stromal cells to improve how much of the added volume survives, aiming for longer-lasting fuller facial or breast contours.
card.note: Specialist surgical procedure; stem-cell processing is regulated differently by country.

quick.overview:
Cell-assisted lipotransfer (CAL) is a variation of autologous fat grafting. Fat taken by liposuction is mixed with stem and stromal cells taken from part of the same patient's fat, then injected where volume is wanted, such as the face or breasts. The aim is for more of the transferred fat to survive, giving a fuller result that lasts.

It was developed in Japan in the mid-2000s. Meta-analyses of clinical studies report higher fat survival with CAL than with standard grafting, particularly in the face, while noting that many included studies were small and not randomised.
quick.how: A surgeon harvests fat by liposuction, processes part of it to obtain a stromal vascular cell fraction or cultured stem cells, combines those cells with the remaining fat, and injects the mixture into the target area. It is performed in specialist clinics under anaesthesia; results are judged over months.
quick.risks: Risks are those of liposuction and fat grafting: swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection and partial resorption. Reviews report similar complication rates between CAL and standard grafting overall, with higher complication rates in breast than face cases. Regulation of cell-processing steps differs between countries.

lead: Cell-assisted lipotransfer (CAL) is a technique in which autologous fat is supplemented with adipose-derived stem or stromal cells before being injected to add volume, most commonly in the face and breasts. Its purpose is to improve graft survival, because conventional fat grafting is associated with resorption rates reported between 20 and 80 percent.[1][2]

Yoshimura and colleagues in Japan introduced the approach around 2006, reporting that aspirated fat is relatively poor in stem cells and can be enriched by adding cells from a portion of the same tissue.[3][4] The method has been applied to facial lipoatrophy, breast augmentation and breast-implant complications, and has been investigated in craniofacial microsomia and radiation-damaged tissue.[5][6][7]

Meta-analyses report higher fat survival with CAL than with standard grafting, while noting heterogeneity between studies.[1][2] A multicentre randomised study of stromal vascular fraction-enriched facial fat grafting has since evaluated safety and efficacy.[8]

Greater share of grafted fat survives

angle.text: CAL is used to add volume to the cheeks, temples, lips or breasts with the patient's own tissue, aiming for more durable fullness than plain fat transfer.

infobox: Patient's own fat plus adipose-derived stromal cells

paras: In CAL, fat is aspirated, a portion is processed to obtain stromal vascular fraction cells, and these cells are combined with the remaining fat before injection. The rationale is that aspirated fat contains few adipose-derived stem cells compared with excised fat, so enrichment may support regeneration and retention.[3][4] Reviews also discuss condensing tissue and cells to improve outcomes when injection volume is limited.[9]

CAL has been used for facial lipoatrophy, where early clinical work reported improved contour,[5] and for breast enhancement or rescue after implant complications.[6] Facial fat grafts are also used for cheek and periorbital volume.

Complications overlap with fat grafting generally, including swelling, bruising and contour irregularity. A 2016 meta-analysis reported similar complication incidence between CAL and standard grafting, higher in breast than in face cases.[2] Reviews discuss regulatory and oncologic questions about stem-cell enrichment.[1][10]
The group of Yoshimura and Matsumoto published the CAL concept in 2006 and its clinical use in 2008.[3][4][5]

A 2016 meta-analysis of 17 articles covering 387 cases found fat survival of about 60 percent with CAL versus 45 percent without, a significant gain in the face (about 19 percent) but a smaller, non-significant gain in the breast; multiple operations were reduced by about 13.6 percent.[2] A 2018 meta-analysis of 25 studies (696 patients) reported survival of 64 percent versus 44 percent.[1] A multicentre randomised controlled study enrolled 23 participants for SVF-enriched facial fat grafting.[8] Smaller trials include a craniofacial microsomia study of 29 participants and a micromastia study of 20.[11][12]

timeline.event: CAL concept published by Yoshimura et al.[3]
Clinical results for facial lipoatrophy and soft-tissue augmentation reported.[4][5]
Meta-analysis of efficacy and safety published.[2]
Multicentre randomised study of SVF-enriched facial grafts published.[8]
